description: Parker-Hannifin Corporation engages in the manufacture and sale of motion and control technologies and systems for aerospace and defense, in-plant and industrial equipment, transportation, off-highway
description_full: Parker-Hannifin Corporation engages in the manufacture and sale of motion and control technologies and systems for aerospace and defense, in-plant and industrial equipment, transportation, off-highway, energy, and HVAC and refrigeration markets in North America, EMEA, Asia Pacific, and Latin America. It operates through two segments: Diversified Industrial and Aerospace Systems. The company offers various motion-control systems and components, such as active and passive vibration control, high purity sealing, coatings, high temperature sealing, cryogenic valves and fittings, HVAC/R controls and monitoring, elastomeric, fabric reinforced, metal, precision cut seals, hydrogen and natural gas filters, electric and hydraulic pumps and motors, industrial air, gas filtration, electric and hydraulic valves, miniature pumps and valves, electromagnetic interface shielding, pneumatic actuators, regulators and valves, electromechanical and hydraulic actuators, power take offs, electronics, drives and controllers, process filtration solutions, engine filtration solutions, rubber to substrate adhesives, fluid condition monitoring, sensors and diagnostics, fluid conveyance hose and tubing, structural adhesives, high pressure connectors, fittings, valves and regulators, thermal management, high purity fittings. The company also provides products for use in commercial and defense airframe and engine programs, such as avionics, electric and hydraulic braking systems, electric power, electromechanical actuators, engine exhaust systems and components, fire detection and suppression, flight control systems, fluid conveyance, fuel systems and components, fuel tank inserting systems, hydraulic pumps and motors, hydraulic valves and actuators, pneumatics, seals, sensors, and thermal management products. The company sells its products to original equipment manufacturers, distributors, direct-sales employees. Parker-Hannifin Corporation was founded in 1917 and is headquartered in Cleveland, Ohio.

financial_summary: Parker-Hannifin Corporation is a large-cap industrials business with a $120.5B market cap on $21.5B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +4% over the past three years and +7% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.

Returns on capital run at 16% against a 10% cost of capital, a 6-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, and 23% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $3.9B in free cash flow — roughly 18 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.20× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.3× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 13× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield is only 1.8%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.1× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

Tariff and trade-policy exposure — industrial exporters sit squarely in the crosshairs of protectionist policy, and retaliatory tariffs can close markets without warning.

sect: Its 24% operating margin runs 15pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.12x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.6% of sector revenue and 1.2% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+7.0% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 548 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 14% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 9% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 13% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 27% and a beta of 1.11, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.65 vs 5y 1.13), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $572.1M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 55% in the 2020 crash, 27% in the 2022 bear market and 67% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $650 (margin of safety -47%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 29%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $493 to $864 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Industrials peers: P/E 32.8 vs 24.1, EV/EBITDA 23.1 vs 13.4 and P/FCF 30.9 vs 22.9 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 72% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.2% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.7% (vs the 8% bar).
The 24 covering analysts target $1,138 on average, 19% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 16% earns above the cost of capital of 9.8%, but the 6pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have been steady (CV 0.21).
It runs a 23% gross margin and converts 18% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.20x.
ROE of 24% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.0x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 5pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 1.2% of revenue on R&D and 0.8% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 1.3x net debt to EBITDA ($501.0M of cash against $7.5B of debt), with interest covered 12.6x.
Goodwill makes up 36% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 4.1% over 3 years, 8.4% over 5 years and 6.6% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 14% of profits supports about 2.2% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 10.5% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.08 (orders outpacing sales) and a backlog worth 60% of annual revenue.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.3x, 2.1% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 26, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.2%), and institutions hold 91%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (6 sales, net $4.3M sold).
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.8% (1.0% in buybacks and 0.8% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 40 consecutive years, raising it 14.5% a year over the last five.
people: With about 59,850 employees, each generates about $359K of revenue, in line with the Industrials median, and revenue has grown 4.9% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $65K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $7.3M (20x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
